title: Friday: ghusl and perfume
tomorrow: one surah gets its own Friday light. which one, and why?

segments.voice: Yesterday the whole day came together, from waking to sleep. Now zoom out one notch. The week has a rhythm too, and it turns on Friday.

The night before a big day, the shirt goes on a hanger and the shoes wait by the door. Now a hot Friday in Medina. The mosque is filling with working people who came in from the outskirts, straight from their jobs, covered in dust and sweat. Aisha remembers it. One of these men comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ while he is at her house, dust and all. A room full of tired workers. What does he tell them?
screen: `THE SHIRT ON THE HANGER.` → `A HOT FRIDAY IN MEDINA.` → `DUST AND SWEAT.` → `WHAT DOES HE SAY?`

segments.voice: He doesn't scold them. In the report Aisha gives, kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, he says: if only you would clean yourselves for this day of yours. This day of yours. Friday is treated as an occasion, something you get ready for. Another report, from Salman, a Persian companion, lays out the whole routine. Wash on Friday. Clean up as well as you can. Put on oil, or perfume from home. Walk to the mosque, and don't squeeze between two people already sitting. Pray what you can, then listen quietly while the imam speaks. And the promise attached: what falls between that Friday and the next is forgiven. A third report adds the toothstick, and perfume if there's any to be had. Notice the order. The bath, the scent, the walk and the listening are one chain with the prayer. The getting ready is part of the worship, not the warm-up before it. The Qur'an names the day al-Jumu'ah, the gathering, and says, in Pickthall's words: "When the call is heard for the prayer of the day of congregation, haste unto remembrance of Allah and leave your trading." Here's something to tell a friend tonight: scholars argue about the bath itself. One report calls it wajib, a duty; another says wudu, the washing before prayer, is enough, and the bath is better. So some schools hold the Friday bath required, and others hold it strongly recommended. Nobody argues for arriving dusty.
screen: `FOR THIS DAY OF YOURS.` · `WASH, SCENT, WALK, LISTEN.` · `READY IS PART OF IT.` · `REQUIRED OR RECOMMENDED?` · then, large: `READY FOR FRIDAY.`

segments.voice: Get one thing ready for your next Friday, right now. Hang a clean shirt where you'll see it, set the little bottle of scent by the door, or put a reminder on the night before. If Friday isn't your day, pick the next day that matters to you and ready one thing for it.
Friday, al-Jumu'ah, the day of gathering: a day you wash and dress for, because the getting ready belongs to it.
Keep this close: ready for friday means washed, scented and on your way before the call. The weekly rhythm, underway.

howItsDone: Muslims who attend the Friday congregational prayer bathe beforehand, put on clean clothes and a little scent, and try to arrive early to listen to the sermon before praying together.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 902 (Aisha: people came from the outskirts covered in dust and sweat; 'if only you would clean yourselves for this day of yours')
Sahih al-Bukhari 883 (Salman al-Farsi: bath, cleaning, oil or perfume, not separating two people, praying, listening; forgiveness until the next Friday)
Sahih al-Bukhari 880 (the Friday bath is wajib for every adult; the toothstick, and perfume if available)
Sunan Abi Dawud 354; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 497 (whoever does wudu on Friday, that is fine; whoever bathes, the bath is better)
